G.B. c. L.Bo.

2014 QCCS 18

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No:

500-17-072427-126

DATE:

THIS 6
th
DAY OF JANUARY, 2014

______________________________________________________________________

THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE MARK G.
PEACOCK, J.S.C.

G. B.
,

Plaintiff

-and-

DALE PARIZEAU MORRIS & MACKENZIE,

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

Introduction

[
1
]

At the time of the incident, Mr. B.
(hereinafter “the Plaintiff”) and Ms Bo. (hereinafter the “Defendant”) were a
couple living together as “
conjoints de fait
”.  On
July 4, 2008, she was driving his 22-ft, 330 horsepower
water-ski boat when she accidentally ran over him after he had
accidentally fallen into the water from a surf board which was being pulled
behind that boat.

[
2
]

He was severely injured and went through a
lengthy period of hospitalization with numerous operations as well as a lengthy
period of rehabilitation at a rehabilitation facility.

[
3
]

In the three years after the accident, she
conscientiously visited him and attended to his needs.

[
4
]

In 2011, the couple separated.  Almost four
years after the accident on June 13, 2012, he instituted legal
proceedings against her, the Defendant Insurance Broker (hereinafter the
“Insurance Broker”) through whom he purchased the boat insurance, as well as
three insurance companies.  These insurance companies are no longer part of the
legal proceedings.

[
5
]

Following several examinations on discovery
before defence, the remaining two defendants, the Defendant and the Insurance
Broker, have taken complementary motions to dismiss and to declare that the
Plaintiff’s proceedings are abusive, in accordance with articles 165(4) and
54.1 and following, C.C.P.

[
6
]

The Defendant alleges that the Plaintiff’s
proceedings should be dismissed firstly on the grounds of prescription and
secondly on the grounds he signed a renunciation of all his rights to take
legal proceedings against her. The Insurance Broker asserts the same grounds
and adds that the Plaintiff’s Re-Amended Introductory Motion and Exhibits do
not disclose any cause of action against it.

[
7
]

The Plaintiff’s Re-Amended Introductory
Motion dated May 2, 2013 claims over $2,000,000.00 in damages against the
Defendants.

[
8
]

This interlocutory judgment will proceed
under the following headings:

A-

Motion to Dismiss,

B-

Defendants’ Positions

b.

Against the Insurance Broker

A-

Motion to Dismiss, article 165 (4), C.C.P.

a.

Governing Law

[
9
]

The applicable legal principles have been
summarized by Madam Justice Catherine La Rosa
in the 2008 case of
Le Breton
v. Dubé
[1]
:

“[19]                  Aux fins d’une
requête en irrecevabilité, le juge doit s’en tenir aux faits  allégués dans la
requête introductive d'instance et aux pièces produites au soutien de celle-ci

[1]
. Il ne peut
prendre en considération une autre procédure qui n’a pas été présentée

[2]
.

[20]           La requête en
irrecevabilité doit être examinée avec beaucoup de réserve. En effet, autant
que possible, il faut éviter de mettre fin prématurément à un procès
considérant les graves conséquences qui découlent du rejet d’une action sans
que la demande ne soit examinée au mérite

[3]
.

[21]           La requête en
irrecevabilité pourra être reçue si la situation est claire, évidente et non
équivoque

[4]
.
Si tel est le cas, alors le juge saisi de la requête est en mesure d’en
apprécier le fondement avec tout autant de justesse que s’il avait à le faire
au fond. En pareille circonstance, le juge peut et doit se prononcer sur le
droit, la procédure en irrecevabilité visant précisément à éviter un débat de
fond inutile et coûteux lorsque le fondement légal du recours, à sa face même,
paraît inexistant

[5]
.

[22]           La requête en
irrecevabilité fondée sur la prescription du recours ne sera accueillie que si
ce moyen apparaît de façon claire et précise sans qu’il soit nécessaire
d’interpréter avec subtilité les nuances de la jurisprudence et de la loi qui
s’applique

[6]
.

[23]           Si la date de
début de la prescription est incertaine, à la lecture des allégations de la
requête introductive, mieux vaut laisser le juge saisi du litige au mérite en
décider

[7]
.”

1
Factory Mutual
Insurance Co
c.
Gérin-Lajoie
,
2003 CanLII 22089 (QC CS)
,
J.E.
2003-2093
(C.S.)

2

,

,

(C.A.)
.

.

.

.

6

B-

Article 54.1, C.C.P. and following

a.

Governing Law

[
10
]

The motion judge’s
power under article 54.1 C.C.P.

must be exercised with prudence so as
not to end litigation prematurely before a plaintiff has a full opportunity to
prove their case at trial:
[2]

As in this case, where the motions to dismiss are before defence, the motion’s
judge must take into account the examinations on discovery and the exhibits and
where a case is clear and has no reasonable chance of success, then it should
be dismissed under article 54.1 C.C.P.

[
11
]

The usual prudence that
a motion’s judge must exercise in dismissing a proceeding under article 54.1
C.C.P. is increased where the applicant seeks to have the demand dismissed as
opposed to the defence, since the plaintiff always has the possibility of
correcting gaps in the examination on discovery by providing better evidence at
trial.

[
12
]

Even where it may be
difficult for a plaintiff to prove certain allegations, the evaluation of
evidence and facts must be left to the trial judge and it is not for a motion’s
judge under article 54.1 C.C.P. to dismiss the plaintiff’s proceeding unless it
is clear that the proceeding is “
manifestly unfounded
”:
[3]

“[39]  The Court of Appeal has made it
clear that the motion's judge must undertake the necessary review where a
precise point of law is raised in a motion to dismiss
[9]

irrespective of the difficulty or complexity of the question and irrespective
of whether there are confusing and disparate facts alleged.

[40] At the same time, a motion's
judge must not prematurely put an end to an action by way of a motion to
dismiss where important facts are still in issue.
[10]

[41] Also, the motion's judge must be
prudent in dealing with prescription where the determination of the starting
day for a prescription to begin (or to be suspended) depends on an appreciation
of the facts.
[11]

[42] The serious degree of analysis
that must be performed by the motion's judge when dealing with a point of law
under article 165 (4) C.C.P. is to be contrasted with the summary analysis that
is required by that same judge when a motion seeking dismissal is based on
article 54.1 C.C.P., since the burden imposed by article 54.2 C.C.P. on the
applicant is to "
summarily establish
that an action or pleading
may

be an improper use of procedure and
may
be improper." (Court's
emphasis)

[43] That a more summary approach
should be taken is confirmed in article 54.3 C.C.P. where the possible choice
of sanctions are noted.”

[9]

Gillet

v.
Arthur
,
2004 CanLII 47873 (QC CA)
,
J.E. 2005-167
(C.A.) at para.
29
.

[10]

Christensen

v.
Archevêque catholique romain de Québec
, 2010 S.C.R. 44 at para. 1
citing with approval the dissent of Mr. Justice Chamberland in the earlier
Court of Appeal decision in the same
case,
2009 QCCA 1349 (CanLII)
, 2009 QCCA 1349 at
para.
129
and following.

[11]

Ibid.

at para. 130 and following.

[
13
]

Finally, the Court of
Appeal has confirmed that while article 165 (4) C.C.P. does not require proof
of impropriety to find that a pleading is “
unfounded in law
”, on the
contrary, article 54.1 requires “
blameworthy conduct” which then requires ‘a
court to tailor a sanction to answer the specific character of the wrongful
behaviour in question’.
[4]

C-

Prescription

a.

Governing law

(i):  What is the law applicable to prescription in
this case: Canadian maritime law or the
Civil Code of Quebec
?

[
14
]

This question is a
complex one.

[
15
]

In the present case,
the parties have stipulated that this incident occurred on the
Rivière-des-Prairies
,
which is a navigable inland waterway separating
Montreal from Île Jésus.

[
16
]

The leading Supreme
Court of Canada
case of
Whitbread v. Walley
et al.
[5]
involved
a plaintiff who was injured when a vessel ran aground while the plaintiff was
onboard.  The Supreme Court of Canada stated the following principles:

a.         “
La responsabilité délictuelle découlant de
l’exploitation négligente d’un bateau de plaisance doit être considérée comme
relevant du domaine du droit maritime canadien et de la compétence législative
fédérale”
; and

b.         that Canadian
maritime law extends to “
activités de ceux qui se livrent directement à la
navigation en empruntant les voies intérieures du Canada”,
including the
use of pleasure boats.

[
17
]

In its subsequent

decision of
Succession Ordon v. Grail
,
[6]

the Supreme Court of Canada reaffirmed that only federal jurisdiction
applied  to Canadian maritime law and this ensured the “
uniformity of
maritime law”
across the country. That Court emphasized:

“
The interference of
provincial statutes with core areas of Canadian maritime law, such as the law
of maritime negligence, would interfere with its historical roots and its
appropriately unique character”
and “
This concern for uniformity is one
reason, amongst others, why the application of provincial statutes of general
application to a maritime negligence claim cannot be permitted”.
[7]

[
18
]

Next, the Supreme Court
of Canada confirmed that Canadian maritime law is constantly evolving and is
constituted from numerous sources: “
statutory and non-statutory, national
and international, common-law and civilian…”
[8]

[
19
]

The
Ordon

judgment
involved dependants’ fatal accident claims arising out of 2 boating
accidents.

[
20
]

On the contrary in the
present case, the Defendant driving the Plaintiff's water-ski boat hit the
Plaintiff, who was in the water, having fallen from the surf board which was
being towed by his water-ski boat.

[
21
]

The parties raised
before this Court the possible application of three different articles of the
Marine Liability Act
:

6.

(1)
If
a person is injured by the fault or neglect of another under circumstances that
entitle the person to recover damages,
the dependants of the injured person

may maintain an action in a court of competent jurisdiction for their loss
resulting from the injury against the person from whom the injured person is
entitled to recover
(this Court’s emphasis).

[…]

14.

(1)
No
action may be commenced under
subsection 6(1)
later than two years
after
the cause of action arose
(this
Court’s emphasis).

[…]

23
.

(1)
No
action may be commenced later than two years after the loss or injury arose to
enforce a claim or lien against
a ship in collision
or its owners in
respect of any loss
to another ship
, its cargo or other property on
board, or any loss of earnings of that other ship, or for damages for loss of
life or personal injury suffered by any person on board that other ship, caused
by the fault or neglect of the former ship, whether that ship is wholly or
partly at fault or negligent
(this
Court’s emphasis).

(2)
A
court having jurisdiction to deal with an action referred to in subsection (1):

(
a
) May, in
accordance with the rules of court, extend the period referred to in that
subsection to the extent and on the conditions that it thinks fit;

[… ]

[
22
]

For the following
reasons, the Court determines none of these articles apply here.

[
23
]

The 2009 Quebec Court of Appeal judgment of
Frugoli v. Services aériens
des Cantons de l’Est inc.
[9]

was a claim by the dependants of two American hunters who were drowned in a
lake in northern Quebec when a boat in which they were passengers capsized.
This dependants’ claim fell squarely within articles 6(1) and
14(1) of the federal
Marine Liability Act
.
[10]

[
24
]

This case clearly
confirms the application of Canadian maritime law where the capsizing of a
single boat was involved. The Court of Appeal also confirmed that provincial
prescription under article 2925 C. C. Q
.
was not
applicable.

[
25
]

Based on this analysis,
the Court concludes that Canadian maritime law, and not the
Civil Code
of Quebec
, governs prescription in the present case of a vessel striking a
person in the water of a navigable inland waterway.

(ii) If Canadian maritime law applies what – if any –
prescription is applicable and if article 140,
Marine Liability Act
,
is applicable, from what date does the prescription begin?

[
26
]

This Court concludes
that since this is neither a claim by dependants nor an accident arising out of
the collision of two vessels, articles 6, 14 and 23,
Marine Liability Act,

do not apply. This conclusion is the same as that found by
Mr. Justice Jacques R. Fournier
in the 2004 decision of
Lebel v. 2427 - 9457 Quebec inc.
[11]

[
27
]

However the
jurisprudence is not uniform.  The 2000 Superior Court
decision of
Deschambault
v. De Bellefeuille

[12]
was
a case involving a collision between two jet-skis, which is effectively
equivalent to a collision of two vessels.  At paragraph 17 of that judgment,
the Court applied then article 572(1) of the
Canada Shipping Act (Loi sur la
marine marchande du Canada)
[13]

(the equivalent of present article 23(1),
Marine Liability Act
)
and said that this article applied even where there was no collision between
two vessels.  With the greatest respect, this is an
obiter dictum
with
which this Court does not agree based upon this Court’s earlier reasoning.

[
28
]

For this same
reasoning, the Court respectfully disagrees with the decision in
Lemieux v. Théorêt
[14]

[
29
]

The judgment of
Rioux v. Begin
,
[15]
involved a plaintiff who,
on August 15, 2004, was injured when being towed while holding onto a
buoy behind one boat when the victim was struck by a second boat.  In that
case, there was no debate before the Court as to what was the proper article in
the
Marine Liability Act
to apply since the parties agreed
article 23(1) applied.  However, this result is at variance with the
2010 Superior Court
decision of
Beaulne v. Martel
[16]
, which
involved an accident on slightly different facts occurring on
July 24, 2007 on a navigable lake in Quebec.  In that case, the
plaintiff was being towed by a jet ski while sitting in an inner tube.  The
injuries were caused when the inner tube with the victim hit a dock coming out
from the shore.  Following argument by the parties, the Court determined that
article 23(1),
Marine Liability Act,
did
not
apply
since the inner tube was not a vessel nor had there been a collision between
vessels, within the meaning of the
Marine Liability Act
.  In
that case, the Court applied article 140,
Marine Liability Act
,
without indicating from what date the prescription started.  That article,
which came into force on September 21, 2009, reads:

“
Except as otherwise provided in this Act or in any other Act of
Parliament, no proceedings under Canadian maritime law in relation to any
matter coming within the class of navigation and shipping may be commenced
later than three years after the day on which the cause of action arises.”

[
30
]

As mentioned, that case
stops short of deciding when the prescription starts when article 140 applies
to a cause of action which arose
before
article 140 came into force.
However,
Beaulne
stands for the proposition that article 140,
Marine Liability Act
,
has application to incidents where a person in the water is injured in a boat
accident which occurred
before
article 140 came into force on Sept. 21,
2009.

[
31
]

This Court determines
that the law supports this general proposition from
Beaulne
based on the
following reasoning.

[
32
]

Firstly, the imposition
of a prescription period is an infringement on a plaintiff's right to institute
an action.  The legislator may impose such a limitation but it must do so in a
way that is clear and unambiguous. Any ambiguity must be decided in favour of a
plaintiff.
[17]

[
33
]

Before article 140,
Marine Liability Act
,
was sanctioned into force on June 23, 2009 and became law 90 days later,
i.e. on September 21, 2009, articles 6, 14 and 23 were the
only statutory dispositions under Canadian maritime law that regulated
prescription.

[
34
]

Also, a Superior Court
cannot impose a prescription period where the federal legislator has chosen not
to do so.  The result for this case is that no prescription applied for the
period from when the cause of action first arose, July 4, 2008 up to Sept. 21,
2009.

[
35
]

For the purpose of
deciding the present Motions, the Court determines that the three year
prescription of article 140 did run in this case from Sept. 21, 2009 up to
Sept. 21, 2012 for the following reasons.

[
36
]

Under Canadian maritime
law before Sept. 21, 2009, the only prescriptions that were legislated were in
matters of collisions between vessels and dependants' claims: article 572 (1)
and articles 646 and 649, Canada Shipping Act, which were later replaced by
article 6, 14 and 23,
Marine Liability Act
.

[
37
]

It was only as of the
coming into force of article 140 that all other claims in relation to Canadian
maritime law had imposed on them a prescription of three years from the date of
the cause of action.

[
38
]

The doctrine on
interpretation is clear that :

“When a new
limitation of action provision comes into force, it may extend or shorten the
period within which an action must be commenced. If the provision comes into
force before the period has lapsed, and if applying it would have the effect of
extinguishing the right of action, then its application to those facts is said
to be purely procedural. In such a case, for both parties, all that is lost or
gained is time. As this analysis shows, the courts are concerned that
individuals be treated fairly. When a person has arranged his or her affairs in
accordance with the law as it exists at the time, it is not fair to make that
person submit to an amended version."
[18]

[
39
]

In application to the
present facts, this means that the Plaintiff's cause of action arose at the
time of the incident but was unaffected by any prescription up to Sept. 21,
2009. On that date, article 140 came into force and the three-year prescription
ran from that date forward, thus treating both parties fairly:

(a)

the Plaintiff, who previously
was not constrained by any prescription, now had to bring his action within 3
years; and

(b)

the Defendants, who were
at the indefinite mercy of the Plaintiff since there was no prescription, now
were able to benefit from a three-year prescription.

[
40
]

The result of this
analysis is that the Plaintiff's claim is not prescribed since it was
instituted within the applicable three-year prescription.

[
41
]

At this point, it is
appropriate to discuss another aspect of the
Lebel

decision.
[
19]
That case involved a
plaintiff who was a passenger in a vessel, who was thrown out of the vessel and
who was then run over by the same vessel’s propeller blade.  On the basis that
article 572(1),
Canada Shipping Act,
did not apply because this was not
a collision between two vessels, the Superior Court relied on article 39 of the

Federal Court Act
to apply prescription from the
Quebec Civil Code
:

[29]    Plus
tard à l’article 39, on peut lire :

« (1) Sauf disposition
contraire d'une autre loi, les règles de droit en matière de prescription qui,
dans une province, régissent les rapports entre particuliers s'appliquent à
toute instance devant la Cour d'appel fédérale ou la Cour fédérale dont le fait
générateur est survenu dans cette province.

2) Le délai de
prescription est de six ans à compter du fait générateur lorsque celui-ci n'est
pas survenu dans une province.

(3) [Abrogé, 1990, ch. 8,
article 10]

L.R. (1985), ch. F-7
,
article 39
; 1990,
ch. 8,
article 10
;
2002, ch. 8,
article 38
. »

[30]
Pour les motifs précédemment énoncés, le Tribunal est d’avis que la
présente affaire ne tombe pas sous l’empire d’une disposition contraire au sens
de l’
article 39
de la
Loi sur la Cour fédérale
. Donc si l’action
était mue en Cour fédérale, la prescription serait celle du
Code civil du
Québec
. Il ne peut en être autrement parce que l’action est prise devant la
Cour supérieure.

[
42
]

The trial judge in the
Frugoli

decision, Mr. Justice Robert Mongeon did not agree with this application of
article 39(1),
Federal Court Act
in
Lebel
,
and said so as
follows:

The prescriptive period
will have to be the same, whether the action is taken before the Federal Court
or before a superior court in Canada.

[
43
]

This Court agrees with
Mr. Justice Mongeon and respectfully disagrees with the approach taken by
in
Lebel
.
In addition to the reason expressed by Mr. Justice Mongeon, this Court adds as
follows. At the time of the accident in the present case – July 4, 2008 – the
federal legislator had chosen not to legislate prescription other than those
specific cases in articles 6, 14 and 23.

[
44
]

The federal legislator
only enacted a prescription which applied to individuals who were hit while in
the water by a vessel as of September 23, 2009, the date of coming into force
of article 140,
Marine Liability Act
.  Accordingly, it is inappropriate
to apply a provincial prescription since that would go directly against the
Supreme Court of Canada and the Quebec Court of Appeal’s admonitions that there
is no place for a province to legislate in Canadian maritime law including in
matters of alleged maritime negligence.
[20]

[
45
]

Therefore, at the time
the cause of action arose – on July 4, 2008 – the Defendants have not proven to
this Court that there was any applicable prescription under the Canadian
maritime law, then in force.

(iii)      Can the prescription be suspended where
there is an “impossibility to act” and, if so, are there sufficient facts to
support such a potential conclusion?

[
46
]

The first issue is: In
the event a three-year prescription applies beginning on September 21, 2009, is
there a Canadian maritime law principle akin to article 2904, C.C.Q
., which
reads:

Prescription does not run
against persons if it is impossible in fact for them to act by themselves or to
be represented by other?

[
47
]

The parties did not
provide the Court with any authorities as to whether such principle existed
under Canadian maritime law.  However, both the Plaintiff and the Defendant did
present arguments on “impossibility” should such a principle exist under
Canadian maritime law.

[
48
]

Again, the uncertainty
of the law in this area means that the final outcome is neither clear nor
certain at this stage and on this basis alone the Defendants’ Motions cannot
succeed at this stage.  Moreover, based on the Court’s earlier findings that
the action was brought within the applicable prescription, it is not necessary
to consider the “impossibility” argument.

[
49
]

However, if the Court
was required to consider this issue, it would find, based on
the reasoning in
Christensen

v. Roman Catholic Archbishop of Quebec,
that the issue of when prescription started to run was
dependent on whether the Plaintiff had the mental and psychological capacity to
comprehend:

“
Les trois éléments nécessaires à
l’exercice de son recours (la faute, le préjudice et le lien de causalité entre
la faute et le préjudice). Ce n’est, en définitive, qu’à compter de ce moment,
que les conditions juridiques du droit de poursuite se trouvent enfin réunies
et que la cause d’action se cristallise”.
[21]

[
50
]

Furthermore, the Court
determines that it is a mixed question of fact and law to be decided by the
trial judge as to whether such “
impossibility
” exists.  On the basis of
the record as constituted before this Court, the Court cannot determine that
the Plaintiff has no chance of success on this argument.

b          Analysis

[
51
]

In contrast to the
excerpts from the Plaintiff’s examination on discovery asserted by the
Defendant, the Plaintiff alleged in paragraph 21 in his Re-Amended Introductory
Motion that his injuries prevented him from being able to comprehend his cause
of action until 2010.

[
52
]

The key question is
whether he had the ability to both comprehend and act upon an understanding of
the three elements required by Mr. Justice Chamberland
in
Christensen
:
fault, prejudice and being able to understand the linkage between the two.

[
53
]

In addition to this
general allegation – which the jurisprudence instructs that the Plaintiff must
be given an opportunity to prove at trial – there is more.  The Plaintiff has
filed as Exhibit P-7, his medical file from the Jewish Rehabilitation Center,
which includes a report by neuropsychologist Chantal Simard which is dated July
15, 2010. At pages 4 and 6 of her report, she provides the following analysis:

“Monsieur
[22]
présente
des lacunes au plan de la planification et de l’organisation.  Il est sujet à
amorcer une tâche de façon impulsive et il a du mal à se donner des stratégies
efficaces pour résoudre une problématique. Il procède plutôt impulsivement par
essai erreur sans planification d’ensemble.  Il lui est difficile de faire des
inférences et des déductions à un niveau abstrait.  Il est démuni pour générer
des stratégies et il risque ainsi d’être très dépourvu en résolution de
problèmes.  Qui plus est, il a tendance à persévérer sur un type de réponse.

L’atteinte des fonctions
exécutives affecte le traitement de l’information verbale tant au niveau de la
compréhension que de l’expression qui le situe au niveau de l’intelligence
limite.  Ainsi une moindre capacité d’abstraction, une difficulté à intégrer
simultanément de multiples concepts, un problème à faire des inférences et à
générer des hypothèses et alternatives, une difficulté à organiser sa pensée et
son discours ainsi qu’à conserver temporairement en mémoire de l’information
affectent le fonctionnement verbal”.

[
54
]

Furthermore, the
transcripts of the Plaintiff’s discoveries before defence provide evidence that
while the Plaintiff had some understanding of his injuries and his involvement
in an accident, he had diminished comprehension of the linkage of fault to his
damages, at least up to the time of the Simard report.

[
55
]

Whether the Plaintiff
has sufficient evidence to prove “impossibility” requires a further assessment
of the facts which the law requires be left to the trial judge to decide.

[
56
]

Accordingly, the
Defendants have not met their burden under article 165(4) or article 54.1 and
following since the Plaintiff’s allegations and evidence create an arguable
case that it was impossible for him to act at least – in the minimum – before
July 15, 2010, the date of Dr. Simard’s report.

Defendants’ positions

The Defendants allege

against her as a result of his signing Exhibit R-1 (which was subsequently
filed as Exhibit P-8 in the Re-Amended Introductory Motion dated May 2, 2013)

The Defendant asserts:

a.

that in his original

the Defendant.
[24]

He did not remember when he signed the document but said it was in the presence

The Defendant’s counsel
examined the Plaintiff in a second examination on discovery on January 31,

On February 19, 2003,

photocopy that was used in the second examination on discovery.  In response to
questions as to whether this was his signature on Exhibit  R-1 , the
Plaintiff admitted:

“
Je ne
sais pas, mais elle semble pas être ma signature.  La date, c’est mon
écriture”.

When asked why he said this

.
contesting his signature on the
document R-1 and confirming that the document he signed related to a

deposit on their house; and

the oral evidence of
the Plaintiff is perplexing.  He does admit on his first examination on
discovery that he signed a document in which he renounced to suing Ms Bo..  In his
second discovery, he says
[30]
that

he
“a mal répondu”
and that he was really referring to the document that
concerns the $47,500.00.  After explaining the location where he signed this

[
59
]

On May 2, 2013, the
Plaintiff filed his Re-Amended Introductory Motion and amongst paragraphs, he

Agissements de Lisa”.
At
paragraph 21.12, he alleges that this renunciation is invalid, amongst other

[
60
]

As a matter of law
under article 165(4) or article 54.1, it must be clear - on the basis of the

61

b.         Governing law

[
77
]

An important statutory
obligation on the Insurance Broker to inform and counsel their client is found
at article 28 of the
Loi sur la distribution des produits et services
financiers
[38]
:

28. Un représentant en assurance doit, avant la conclusion d'un
contrat d'assurance, décrire le produit proposé au client en relation avec les
besoins identifiés et lui préciser la nature de la garantie offerte.

•

Il doit, de plus, indiquer clairement au client les exclusions de
garantie particulières compte tenu des besoins identifiés, s'il en est, et lui
fournir les explications requises sur ces exclusions.

[
78
]

Further applicable
legal principles are succinctly summarized by Madam Justice Marie-Anne Paquette
in
125057 Canada Inc. pour Tricots L.G. Ltée v. Fernand Rondeau et Poitras,
Larue, Rondeau Inc.
[39]

:

44.        Il
est bien établi qu'un courtier d'assurances a l'obligation d'informer et de
conseiller son client, afin de lui permettre de prendre des décisions éclairées
et réfléchies. Il n'est pas un simple vendeur ou courroie de transmission entre
l'assuré et l'assureur, mais un professionnel de l'assurance
35
.

45.

À ce titre, il
se doit d'agir avec probité, compétence et professionnalisme pour accomplir son
devoir de renseignement et de conseil. Tant la législation spécifique à ce
domaine
36
que la
jurisprudence
37
vont dans ce
sens. La juge Wilson, écrivant pour la Cour dans Fletcher
38
, s'exprime ainsi au
sujet des obligations des agents et courtiers d'assurances:

•

Il est tout à fait légitime, à mon sens, d'imposer aux agents
et aux courtiers d'assurances privés une obligation stricte de fournir à leurs
clients des renseignements et des conseils.
Ils sont, après
tout, des professionnels agréés qui se sont spécialisés dans l'évaluation des
risques au profit des clients et dans la négociation de polices personnalisées.
Ils offrent un service très personnalisé, axé sur les besoins de chaque client.

La personne ordinaire a souvent de la difficulté à comprendre les
différences subtiles entre les diverses protections offertes.
Les agents et
les courtiers ont reçu une formation qui les rend aptes à saisir ces
différences et à fournir des conseils adaptés à la situation de chaque
individu. Il est à la fois raisonnable et opportun de leur imposer l'obligation
non seulement de fournir des renseignements mais encore de conseiller les
clients. [Soulignements ajoutés]

46.

Ainsi, le
courtier ne peut se contenter d'attendre des questions qui ne viennent pas,
mais qu'il aurait lui-même dû susciter
39
. Les
recommandations formulées doivent aussi être raisonnables et données
clairement, pour éviter une méprise chez l'assuré
40
.

47
.
Cependant,
comme en matière de courtage de valeurs mobilières, les courtiers ne sont pas
tenus de donner les recommandations qui se révèlent idéales, en rétrospective.
L'intensité des obligations varie en fonction des circonstances, dont la nature
du mandat confié par l'assuré et les informations qu'il fournit

The legal positions of
the Insurance Broker were well-argued on behalf of the Insurance Broker.
However, at this formative stage of the proceedings, the Insurance Broker has not
shown that the Plaintiff has no clear chance of proving that the fault
committed was that he was not properly counselled by the Insurance Broker in
regard to his needs i.e. insurance needs for his own personal injury.

[
80
]

In the letter sent by
the
Insurance Broker with the
original policy dated September 27, 2007 – a letter sent to the Defendant and
not to the Plaintiff – the Insurance Broker said to the insured:

“Nous vous conseillons de
vérifier si les garanties prévues par votre contrat répondent encore à vos
besoins et si les montants sont suffisants”.

[
81
]

It is a mixed question
of fact and law – which can only properly be assessed by the trial judge – as
to what actual advice and counsel the Plaintiff received before contracting the
original policy and whether the
Insurance Broker can attenuate any legal obligation to counsel and inform
by putting the responsibility back on the insured as per the September 27, 2007
letter.  Moreover, the letter which sent the second policy and which was
received only
after
the incident noted the following:

a. that the insurer offered a ‘couverture spécialement
adaptée aux besoins des plaisanciers’;

b.  that the insurer was specialized in marine
matters;

c.  “Nous vous invitons à lire attentivement les
documents joints et à nous faire part de tout changement”.

Clearly the applicability of this clause
would be a question to be debated at trial since the letter and the policy were
only received
after
the incident in question.

[
82
]

The
Insurance Broker has not proven to this
Court that the pleadings and exhibits disclose no fault and nor do the
transcripts of the examinations on discovery show any abuse within the context
of article 54.1, as required by the jurisprudence.

[
83
]

For these reasons, the
Insurance Broker’s Motions are dismissed.
